name: Anonymity & Censorship Resistance
description: Anonymous communication (Tor, mix nets) and tools to detect or circumvent censorship.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this set, all from USENIX Security 2018, map out the core tensions of anonymity and censorship resistance. Some probe whether privacy tools deliver on their promises: "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) showed that Zcash's much-touted anonymity often collapses in practice once usage heuristics are applied, while "How Do Tor Users Interact With Onion Services?" (USENIX 2018) studied the usability gap that undermines anonymity in the wild. Others turned outward to the censor: "Quack: Scalable Remote Measurement of Application-Layer Censorship" (USENIX 2018) pushed censorship measurement past DNS- and IP-blocking to the application layer at global scale, and "Effective Detection of Multimedia Protocol Tunneling using Machine Learning" (USENIX 2018) signaled an emerging theme — that machine learning would become the censor's and the analyst's sharpest tool. Performance and resilience of Tor itself were also on the agenda, from circuit prediction to the bandwidth denial-of-service study "Point Break" (USENIX 2019).

Around 2020-2021 the field's center of gravity shifted toward website fingerprinting (WF) and the adversarial machine-learning arms race it spawned. "Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2020) sought practical defenses that did not destroy Tor's performance, and "Defeating DNN-Based Traffic Analysis Systems in Real-Time With Blind Adversarial Perturbations" (USENIX 2021) reframed both fingerprinting and flow correlation as a deep-learning game where adversarial perturbations could blind the classifier. In parallel, censorship circumvention matured into infrastructure-level evasion: "Balboa" (USENIX 2021) tunneled traffic through real application streams, and "Domain Shadowing" (USENIX 2021) repurposed CDNs for blocking-resistant communication. The community also grew more rigorous and more human-centered, with "Once is Never Enough" (USENIX 2021) establishing sound statistical foundations for Tor experimentation and "Collective Information Security in Large-Scale Urban Protests" (USENIX 2021) grounding the threat model in the lived experience of Hong Kong protesters.

By 2022-2023 the WF arms race intensified — "Online Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2022) stress-tested attacks under realistic conditions, and "Subverting Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Robust Traffic Representation" (USENIX 2023) showed defenses still falling to better feature representations. Measurement work sharpened on the censor's machinery, with "Many Roads Lead To Rome" (USENIX 2022) exposing how packet-header choices bias DNS censorship measurement and the landmark "How the Great Firewall of China Detects and Blocks Fully Encrypted Traffic" (USENIX 2023) reverse-engineering exactly how the GFW flags fully-encrypted protocols — directly informing the next generation of obfuscation. Automated and detection-resistant evasion arrived via "GET /out" (USENIX 2022) and "DeResistor" (USENIX 2023).

The most recent USENIX 2024-2025 papers show a field that is simultaneously consolidating and pushing toward provable guarantees. "Snowflake" (USENIX 2024) documented a deployed, ultra-light WebRTC-proxy circumvention system serving real users, while "SpotProxy" (USENIX 2024) tackled the economics of hosting proxies, and "Bridging Barriers" (USENIX 2024) surveyed the whole circumvention-tool ecosystem and its priorities. The cat-and-mouse continues — "Fingerprinting Obfuscated Proxy Traffic with Encapsulated TLS Handshakes" (USENIX 2024) shows obfuscation remains attackable — but "A Framework for Designing Provably Secure Steganography" (USENIX 2025) marks an aspiration to move beyond heuristic obfuscation toward formal, provable undetectability, suggesting where the area is headed next.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work shown here treats Tor's anonymity as something to be measured and probed from the inside. "Inside Job: Applying Traffic Analysis to Measure Tor from Within" (NDSS 2018) showed that adversaries running only middle relays can learn a surprising amount about the network, while "Automated Website Fingerprinting through Deep Learning" (NDSS 2018) marked the moment traffic-analysis attacks moved from hand-crafted features to neural networks, dramatically raising the accuracy with which an eavesdropper could guess which page a Tor user was visiting. Together these framed the two enduring threads of the area: de-anonymizing the people who use privacy tools, and the arms race between attackers and defenders over what traffic reveals.

By 2019-2020 the center of gravity shifted from attacking Tor to the geopolitics of censorship itself. "Decentralized Control: A Case Study of Russia" (NDSS 2020) and "Measuring the Deployment of Network Censorship Filters at Global Scale" (NDSS 2020) turned censorship into an empirical, measurable phenomenon, while a cluster of systems work tackled how to get around it: "The use of TLS in Censorship Circumvention" (NDSS 2019), "SymTCP: Eluding Stateful Deep Packet Inspection with Automated Discrepancy Discovery" (NDSS 2020) which automatically found packet sequences that fool deep packet inspection, "Detecting Probe-resistant Proxies" (NDSS 2020) from the censor's side, and "MassBrowser: Unblocking the Censored Web for the Masses, by the Masses" (NDSS 2020) as a crowd-sourced circumvention design. This period established that circumvention is fundamentally a cat-and-mouse game measured at real-world, global scale.

The more recent NDSS work (2023-2025) splits along two lines. On the anonymity side, attention moved to mix networks and their core tension between latency and privacy, with "LARMix: Latency-Aware Routing in Mix Networks" (NDSS 2024) and "LAMP: Lightweight Approaches for Latency Minimization in Mixnets" (NDSS 2025), alongside continued attacks like "Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Onion Service Sessions with Sliding Subset Sum" (NDSS 2024). On the censorship side, researchers kept auditing real deployments, most strikingly "Wallbleed: A Memory Disclosure Vulnerability in the Great Firewall of China" (NDSS 2025), which found an exploitable buffer over-read inside China's national censorship infrastructure itself.

The 2026 papers show the area broadening in every direction at once. Website fingerprinting remains a hotbed, now grappling with realism and robustness in "CELLSHIFT: RTT-Aware Trace Transduction for Real-World Website Fingerprinting" (NDSS 2026) and "Enhancing Website Fingerprinting Attacks against Traffic Drift" (NDSS 2026), answered by information-theoretic defenses like "Cease at the Ultimate Goodness: Towards Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defense via Iterative Mutual Information Minimization" (NDSS 2026). Circumvention has grown more covert with "Huma: Censorship Circumvention via Web Protocol Tunneling with Deferred Traffic Replacement" (NDSS 2026) and "Mirage: Private, Mobility-based Routing for Censorship Evasion" (NDSS 2026), while de-anonymization pushed beyond Tor to "Time will Tell: Large-scale De-anonymization of Hidden I2P Services" (NDSS 2026). Perhaps the clearest sign of where the field is heading is "Characterizing the Implementation of Censorship Policies in Chinese LLM Services" (NDSS 2026), which extends censorship research from the network layer up into the large language models that increasingly mediate what people can read and say.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice sets a theoretical anchor: "Anonymity Trilemma: Strong Anonymity, Low Bandwidth Overhead, Low Latency - Choose Two" (S&P 2018) proved that anonymous communication systems cannot have all three properties at once, framing every practical design decision that follows as a trade-off rather than an oversight. Around 2020 the field turned sharply empirical. "ICLab: A Global, Longitudinal Internet Censorship Measurement Platform" (S&P 2020) built infrastructure to observe censorship worldwide over time, while "High Precision Open-World Website Fingerprinting" (S&P 2020) showed that an eavesdropper watching only encrypted packet metadata could identify the pages a Tor user visits with alarming precision. A parallel thread checked the math behind the tools themselves, as "Breaking and (Partially) Fixing Provably Secure Onion Routing" (S&P 2020) found gaps in supposedly rigorous onion-routing proofs.

The 2022-2023 period became an arms race between traffic-analysis attacks and defenses. "DeepCoFFEA: Improved Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor via Metric Learning and Amplification" (S&P 2022) used deep learning to link the two ends of a Tor circuit, and "Robust Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attacks in the Wild" (S&P 2023) pushed fingerprinting toward realistic browsing. Defenders answered with "Surakav: Generating Realistic Traces for a Strong Website Fingerprinting Defense" (S&P 2022) and the sobering stock-taking of "SoK: A Critical Evaluation of Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defenses" (S&P 2023), which questioned how well existing defenses actually hold up. At the same time, censorship resistance branched into unobservable covert channels that hide inside ordinary applications — "Telepath: A Minecraft-based Covert Communication System" (S&P 2023) and "Discop: Provably Secure Steganography in Practice" (S&P 2023) — moving beyond Tor toward traffic that a nation-state censor cannot easily flag at all.

By 2024 the work matured into deployable systems and closer study of Tor's own machinery: "NetShuffle: Circumventing Censorship with Shuffle Proxies at the Edge" (S&P 2024), "Pudding: Private User Discovery in Anonymity Networks" (S&P 2024), and "Attacking and Improving the Tor Directory Protocol" (S&P 2024) all pair a concrete attack or weakness with a fix. Website fingerprinting kept escalating with real-time defenses like "Real-Time Website Fingerprinting Defense via Traffic Cluster Anonymization" (S&P 2024).

The most recent papers show the area splitting into several confident sub-fields at once. Censorship measurement grew more granular and adversary-aware — "A Wall Behind A Wall: Emerging Regional Censorship in China" (S&P 2025) documents censorship layered within a single country, and 2026 brings machine-driven measurement and user-facing alerting with "CenRL: A Framework for Performing Intelligent Censorship Measurements" (S&P 2026) and "CenAlert: Amplifying User Voices to Rally Censorship Investigation" (S&P 2026). Fingerprinting attacks keep advancing via "Countmamba" (S&P 2025), while anonymity research now stretches from provably optimal mixnet leakage analysis in "Mixnets on a Tightrope" (S&P 2025) to human-centered questions in "Usable Anonymity in Reproductive Health Privacy" (S&P 2026). And Tor itself remains under active attack, with "Descriptors of Exposure: Undermining Tor Anonymity Through Exploiting Descriptor Flood" (S&P 2026) and latency experiments like "SaTor: Exploring Satellite Routing in Tor to Reduce Latency" (S&P 2026) still probing the same trilemma the 2018 paper first drew.

ccs.narrative:
Anonymity and censorship resistance at CCS has been defined by the Tor ecosystem—fingerprinting attacks, flow correlation, and defenses—alongside global censorship measurement. Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning (CCS 2018) set a high-water mark by defeating every then-current Tor defense with a CNN. DeepCorr: Strong Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Using Deep Learning (CCS 2018) showed flow correlation attacks could reliably deanonymize Tor users using deep learning on traffic patterns. Both papers drove a defensive research surge.

Defensive innovation followed: TrafficSliver: Fighting Website Fingerprinting Attacks with Traffic Splitting (CCS 2020) proposed routing Tor traffic across multiple entry guards to disrupt fingerprinting features. Measuring Information Leakage in Website Fingerprinting Attacks and Defenses (CCS 2018) provided an information-theoretic framework for evaluating these attacks quantitatively. Censored Planet: An Internet-wide, Longitudinal Censorship Observatory (CCS 2020) brought systematic measurement infrastructure to global censorship, tracking reachability across countries and protocols continuously.

By 2023, deep learning attack capability had grown further: Realistic Website Fingerprinting By Augmenting Network Traces (CCS 2023) made attacks more robust by augmenting training data, and Transformer-based Model for Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attack (CCS 2023) extended fingerprinting to multi-tab browsing scenarios. The community had not yet produced a defense that matched attacker pace.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, from 2018, split cleanly along two lines that still define the area. On the theory side, "Anonymity Trilemma: Strong Anonymity, Low Bandwidth Overhead, Low Latency - Choose Two" (S&P 2018) proved a fundamental tension: no anonymous communication system can deliver strong anonymity, low latency, and low overhead all at once. On the attack side, deep learning arrived with force. "Deep Fingerprinting" (CCS 2018) and "DeepCorr: Strong Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Using Deep Learning" (CCS 2018) showed that neural networks could identify the pages a Tor user visits and correlate flows across the network far better than prior hand-tuned methods, while "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) exposed how weakly the anonymity of privacy coins held up in practice. A parallel censorship-measurement thread also opened, with "Quack: Scalable Remote Measurement of Application-Layer Censorship" (USENIX 2018) pushing detection to global scale.

The next few years turned single results into two maturing sub-fields. Website fingerprinting became a genuine arms race: "Triplet Fingerprinting" (CCS 2019) made attacks portable across settings with few examples, and defenders answered with "Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2020) and "TrafficSliver" (CCS 2020), which split traffic across paths to blur the signal. Meanwhile censorship research shifted from one-off studies to continuous, planet-scale observation, anchored by "Censored Planet" (CCS 2020) and "ICLab" (S&P 2020), and to automated evasion with "Geneva: Evolving Censorship Evasion Strategies" (CCS 2019), which evolved evasion tactics automatically. Country-focused studies like "Decentralized Control: A Case Study of Russia" (NDSS 2020) showed censorship taking new architectural forms, and "Practical Traffic Analysis Attacks on Secure Messaging Applications" (NDSS 2020) reminded the field that even Signal and Telegram leak through timing.

By the early 2020s the attack-defense loop tightened and grew more realistic. "DeepCoFFEA" (S&P 2022) made flow correlation scalable, and attacks moved out of the lab toward messy conditions: "Online Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2022) and "Robust Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attacks in the Wild" (S&P 2023) tackled real browsing with multiple open tabs, while "Subverting Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Robust Traffic Representation" (USENIX 2023) broke defenses once again. Defenders pushed back with trace-generation approaches like "Surakav" (S&P 2022) and took stock in "SoK: A Critical Evaluation of Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defenses" (S&P 2023), which questioned how well efficient defenses actually hold.

The most recent work, clustered at NDSS 2026, shows the field confronting real-world drift and expanding its targets. Several papers wrestle with keeping fingerprinting practical as conditions change over time and across networks, including "Enhancing Website Fingerprinting Attacks against Traffic Drift" and "CELLSHIFT: RTT-Aware Trace Transduction for Real-World Website Fingerprinting," while defenses grow more principled in "Cease at the Ultimate Goodness: Towards Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defense via Iterative Mutual Information Minimization." De-anonymization has moved beyond Tor: "Time will Tell: Large-scale De-anonymization of Hidden I2P Services via Live Behavior Alignment" attacks I2P hidden services at scale, and mixnet anonymity gets fresh scrutiny in "When Mixnets Fail" and "OptiMix." On the censorship side, "Huma" and "Mirage" pursue new circumvention channels, while "Characterizing the Implementation of Censorship Policies in Chinese LLM Services" signals a striking new front — censorship now embedded inside large language model platforms, not just the network.
